articleTitle: AI’s Money‑Making Promise Stalls Outside Tech, Apollo Economist Reports

claims.claim: Apollo Global Management’s chief economist, Torsten Slok, released a note that casts doubt on the financial upside of artificial intelligence for most U.S. companies.

claims.evidence: Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo Global Management, published a note on October 24 making a specific, checkable claim: revenue per worker and profit margins have climbed for the Magnificent Seven since the AI spending wave began, and have stayed essentially flat for the other 493 companies in the S&P 500.

editorial.claim: Slok’s note highlights that the growth seen by the broader market is confined to these “Magnificent 7.” The top 10% of firms account for 99.5% of model‑serving and inference spend, and 80.4% of the highest‑spending companies are venture‑backed.
Slok’s research suggests that, outside the tech sector, AI has delivered “zero payoff” to corporate America.
Therefore, while the overall trend is clear—flat margins for the S&P 493—the precise magnitude of any marginal improvements remains uncertain.
Additionally, the concentration of AI spend among venture‑backed firms suggests that the broader economy’s exposure to AI risk may be limited to a small, high‑growth sector.
Investors and corporate leaders should monitor whether the flat margins for the S&P 493 hold as AI adoption matures.
